title: TA9-20136
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXX XXXXX claims Convention refugee status by reasons of his membership in a particular social group and/or actual or perceived political opinion. The claimant claims that due to his father's political activities, he is being targeted by political opponents and the government of Tanzania. He is also claiming that he is a person in need of protection in accordance with sections 97(1) (a) and (b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1 ALLEGATIONS
According to the claimant, he is a citizen of Tanzania.

In the Personal Information Form, it is noted that the claimant's parents are fearful for their safety "due to threats on my Father life [sic] by his political opponents and the government security agencies."2 As the eldest son, the claimant fears that he will also be targeted.
The claimant arrived in Canada on XXXXX XXXXX, 2005 and requested refugee protection in land on October 14, 2009.

A Notice to Appear for a Scheduling Conference, dated March 2, 2011, was served on the claimant at his address of XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, for his attendance on March 21, 2011. The claimant attended the conference and noting that he did not have counsel, was informed of his right to counsel. As well, the definition of a Convention refugee was explained and he was provided with a hearing date of June 23, 2011.

A peremptory Notice to Appear and a Statement of Service were sent to the claimant's last known addresses, which was the same as noted above, on March 24, 2011. The claimant did not attend the hearing, scheduled for 12:58 PM, or provide reasons for his absence in writing. Nor was the Notice to Appear and Statement of Service returned to the Immigration and Refugee Board. The Panel commenced abandonment proceedings.

The Board received a medical report from a dentist on XXXXX, 2011 at 1:47 PM., indicating that the claimant was undergoing a dental procedure and required time off work. This medical report was forwarded to the Board after the Panel commenced abandonment proceedings.

A Notice to Appear - Abandonment of a Claim for Refugee Protection and a Statement of Service, dated August 23, 2011, was sent to the claimant's home address and a copy was also sent to his recently retained lawyer, Mr. Adetayo Akinyemi. The hearing was scheduled for 1:00 P.M. on October 5, 2011. Neither the claimant nor his lawyer attended, nor were written reasons provided for their lack of attendance. The Panel declared the claim abandoned on October 5, 2011.

On October 6, 2011, at approximately 9 AM, the Immigration and Refugee Board, Refugee Protection Division received a faxed letter from Dr. XXXXX, dated XXXXX, 2011 stating that the claimant required "some days off work" because he had a migraine headache. The Panel never received this medical report until December 22, 2011.
The Federal Court of Canada A/Senior Registry Officer, in a Request to the Tribunal, dated November 29, 2011, requested a copy of written reasons with respect to the abandonment determination.

The Notice to Appear - Abandonment of a Claim for Refugee Protection, states, in part, that: Important Instructions If you fail to appear at that time and place to explain why your claim should not be determined abandoned, the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) may determine your claim to have been abandoned. This means that you would lose the right to have your claim heard by the RPD.

Section 168(1) of the IRPA3 states: 168. (1) A Division may determine that a proceeding before it has been abandoned if the Division is of the opinion that the applicant is in default in the proceedings, including by failing to appear for a hearing, to provide information required by the Division or to communicate with the Division on being requested to do so.

Abandonment Proceedings are guided by Rule 58,4 which indicates that: Abandonment without hearing the claimant 58. (1) A claim may be declared abandoned, without giving the claimant an opportunity to explain why the claim should not be declared abandoned, if the Division has not received the claimant's contact information and their Personal Information Form within 28 days after the claimant received the form; and (b) the Minister and the claimant's counsel, if any, do not have the claimant's contact information. Opportunity to explain (2) In every other case, the Division must give the claimant an opportunity to explain why the claim should not be declared abandoned. The Division must give this opportunity immediately, if the claimant is present at the hearing and the Division considers that it is fair to do so; or (b) in any other case, by way of a special hearing after notifying the claimant in writing. Factors to consider (3) The Division must consider, in deciding if the claim should be declared abandoned, the explanations given by the claimant at the hearing and any other relevant information, including the fact that the claimant is ready to start or continue the proceedings. Decision to start or continue the proceedings (4) If the Division decides not to declare the claim abandoned, it must start or continue the proceedings without delay.

The claimant sought the protection of Canada upon submission of his claim for refugee status. Thus, it is his obligation to proceed with the claim when called upon to do so. He, therefore, has an obligation to provide all necessary information to the Immigration and Refugee Board, Refugee Protection Division, and appear for scheduled hearings ready to proceed. As noted by the Federal Court in Capelos,5 "an individual has a responsibility to take initiative and actively pursue the claim being made. It is not sufficient to place oneself in a position where communication is difficult or non-existent and then plead lack of knowledge of what occurred, as a ground for seeking an extension of time." In the case at hand, the claimant did not provide medical information until after the scheduled hearings. Mr. Akinyemi, the claimant's lawyer, specializes in immigration law and is or should be knowledgeable with respect to proceedings before the Refugee Protection Division. Mr. Akinyemi did not attend the hearing or send an agent on his behalf. The Panel finds that the claimant has failed to fulfill his obligation to diligently pursue his claim for refugee protection.

When a claimant is in default with respect to the Refugee Protection Division proceedings, he has the onus of justifying his actions in a timely manner. He is therefore required to provide a cogent explanation for his default, which, as noted above, the claimant failed to do at the hearing of June 23, 2011. In addition, he must satisfy the Panel, on a balance of probabilities, as to his intention to pursue the claim with diligence; which he also failed to do. The Panel is not satisfied that the claimant and his representative's conduct amounted to an expression of intention that they were prepared to pursue this claim with diligence. The lack of appearance and lack of timely explanation on both dates of hearing resulted in the Board incurring unnecessary expense and increased administrative duties. Thus, there has been no reasonable expression of intention to pursue the claimant's claim with diligence.

In accordance with Rule 58 (3), the claimant has failed, based on a balance of probabilities, to establish that his claim for refugee protection has been pursued in a diligent manner, and the claim is therefore declared abandoned.

The Panel determines that the claimant's claim for Convention refugee and person in need of protection status in accordance with sections 96 and 97(1)(a) and (b) of the IRPA has been declared abandoned.
